bridge: You know processes, files and networking. Start with the lab diagram and identify which resources belong only to the exercise.
teaching:
### Compare two kinds of isolation

A virtual machine runs a guest operating system using virtualised hardware. A container normally shares the host kernel while separating selected resources. They are useful for different jobs and do not promise identical isolation.

A container image packages a filesystem and metadata. Running it creates a process with the permissions and connections you grant. A trusted-looking image name is not proof that every included program is safe.

### Check what crosses the boundary

A shared folder or mounted volume exposes host files to the lab. Published ports can expose lab services to other devices. Credentials and environment variables can give the lab access beyond the host itself.

Write down every deliberate connection. Prefer only the folders, ports and permissions the exercise actually needs. An isolated-looking window can still have access to important host resources.

### Use snapshots with clear limits

A snapshot records a recoverable state under the platform's rules. It can help restore a lab after a change. It may not undo actions on external services or erase files already copied elsewhere.

### Make the target unmistakable

Name the permitted targets and check the network mode before beginning. Use fictional inputs and disposable lab data. If a command points outside that environment, stop and resolve the target rather than treating the whole internet as part of the lab.
example:
Lab plan (paper fixture)
Host: your own computer
Guest: supported training Linux VM
Network: NAT or isolated mode chosen for the exercise
Shared folders: none initially
Credentials: invented lab-only values
Baseline: clean-setup snapshot
Recovery check: create marker.txt, restore baseline, confirm marker absent
Exposed app: loopback only unless the lab explicitly requires otherwise
explanation: The marker test checks restoration behaviour without introducing hostile software. It does not prove that every disk or external volume is covered by the snapshot. Record which state is excluded. NAT connectivity is not an automatic assurance that all traffic or inbound access is forbidden.
exercise: Produce the full lab plan introduced in Learn for your selected platform. If a supported VM is available, perform the harmless marker restore. Otherwise complete the paper plan and explicitly label the runtime restore check unperformed; do not mark it as verified.
solution: Example paper plan: supported Linux guest from the training provider’s official image; record exact image version and download source; allocate RAM/disk within that platform’s documented requirements and your available capacity; choose an isolated lab network; no shared folders, clipboard sharing or personal credentials; name the clean snapshot baseline. Create marker.txt inside the guest, restore baseline, and record whether the marker disappeared if you actually perform the test. List excluded external disks/services. If no VM is available, label the entire restore observation unperformed and retain the completed paper design.
challenge: Compare two proposed labs: A mounts your entire home directory writable into a container; B uses a clean VM with no shared folders and invented data. Explain the extra exposure in A and propose a minimal change.
challenge_solution: A grants access to unrelated personal files and expands consequences of a compromised process. Remove the broad mount, share only an explicit disposable directory if needed and choose a VM boundary for workloads that require it. Neither configuration is a universal containment guarantee.
example_intro: This is a lab-planning checklist, not a ready-made virtual machine. Choose an officially supported training image and the setup instructions for your own platform before any runtime task. Snapshot and network controls depend on that platform.
